issues.legal_issue: A legislature cannot retrospectively acquire property by a provision that directly nullifies a final judgment without changing the legal basis on which that judgment rests.
material_facts: A final judgment had declared the acquisition notices invalid and directed that the factories be returned to their owners.
A later amendment declared that the ten factories listed in its schedule stood transferred to the government, notwithstanding any judgment, and validated actions taken in relation to those factories.
The amendment did not alter the legal basis on which the earlier judgment had found the acquisition process invalid.
The factories were not acquired under the ordinary statutory acquisition provisions, and the scheduled acquisition provision did not provide notice, a hearing, or comparable safeguards.
issues.conclusion: The scheduled acquisition provision was unconstitutional because it directly displaced a final judgment without curing the defect underlying that judgment; acquisition could not be effected through that provision without the required procedural safeguards.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 245 and 141 of the Constitution, the legislature makes law while courts declare the law. A legislature may retrospectively change the law and remove or alter the legal basis of a judicial decision, but it cannot simply declare a final decision between parties invalid or displace it without curing the defect on which it rests. Acquisition must also observe the rules of natural justice. The Court relied on State of T.N. v. M. Rayappa Gounder (1971) 3 SCC 1; D. Cawasji and Co. Mysore v. State of Mysore (1985) 1 SCR 825; State of Haryana v. Karnal Coop. Farmers’ Society Ltd. (1993) 2 SCC 363; Re Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 96; S.R. Bhagwat v. State of Mysore (1995) 6 SCC 16; and Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan (1996) 2 SCC 449.

rule.if: legislative_override_challenge and final_judgment_directed_return and later_law_expressly_overrides_judgment and underlying_defect_uncured

predicates.legislative_override_challenge: The case challenges a law that purports to validate a prior acquisition after a final adjudication concerning that acquisition.
predicates.final_judgment_directed_return: A final judgment between the affected parties directed return of the property after finding a defect in the acquisition process.
predicates.later_law_expressly_overrides_judgment: A later law purports to vest the same property despite the final judgment.
predicates.underlying_defect_uncured: The later law does not change or cure the legal defect on which the final judgment rested.

issues.definition: When a challenged law purports to reverse a final order returning property and leaves the defect underlying that order uncured, the acquisition provision is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A law that treats similarly situated acquired properties differently violates equality when the distinction has no rational relation to the law’s objective.
material_facts: The state had issued notices in identical terms to 46 factories, and the factories were similarly situated for the purpose of the stated objective of avoiding unemployment among cashew workers.
The amendment placed ten factories in its schedule for acquisition but did not do so for the other 36 factories.

The different management bodies operating the two groups did not distinguish them in relation to the objective of avoiding worker unemployment; both groups involved unemployment concerns and potential financial loss to the government and the managing bodies.
issues.conclusion: The distinction between the ten scheduled factories and the other 36 factories had no intelligible differentia rationally related to the objective and violated Article 14; the acquisition provision was therefore unconstitutional on this ground as well.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification only where it rests on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court found no such distinction between the two groups of factories. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_acquisition_classification and affected_groups_similarly_situated and only_one_group_selected and group_difference_unrelated_to_object

predicates.equality_challenge_to_acquisition_classi: The case challenges a law that selects some acquired properties for different treatment on equality grounds.
predicates.affected_groups_similarly_situated: The properties in the groups are similarly situated in relation to the objective the law seeks to achieve.
predicates.only_one_group_selected: The law selects one group for the challenged treatment but excludes the comparable group.
predicates.group_difference_unrelated_to_object: Any difference between the groups does not rationally relate to the law’s stated objective.

issues.definition: When a challenged classification selects only one of two similarly situated groups and their difference is unrelated to the law’s objective, the classification violates equal protection.
